China at risk of 20% youth joblessness as labour distress spreads
article:
(July 21): China’s unemployment among young people could be headed for levels last seen more than three years ago, as a record number of graduates prepare to enter the labour market at a time when AI is threatening to displace more entry-level jobs.

Surveyed unemployment in urban areas for those aged 16-24 came in at 14.9% last month, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics this week. While extending a pattern of seasonal decline, it was the highest for June since the government excluded university students from the sample more than two years ago after the rate surpassed 20%.

Youth joblessness typically bottoms out in June before spiking later in the summer as more graduates join the labour market. An unprecedented 12.7 million of students are set to enter the workforce this year, according to the Ministry of Education, an increase of nearly 4% from 2025.

Zhaopeng Xing, an economist with Australia & New Zealand Banking Group, expects youth unemployment to approach 20% in the next two months as a labour “oversupply” worsens. “Employment pressure is still growing due to both cyclical and structural challenges,” said Xing, pointing to factors such as weak domestic demand and the adoption of artificial intelligence in the workplace.

The bleak job prospects facing China’s youth crystallise the challenge ahead for officials after economic growth weakened more than expected in the second quarter to below Beijing’s annual target. With consumption and investment remaining sluggish, the spread of AI is ushering in a transformation that Citigroup Inc predicts could eventually threaten to displace an estimated 70 million workers in China.

See also: Hong Kong court rejects water heiress appeal over US$1.8 bil

China’s AI adoption rate is the highest in Asia and above that for the US, according to analysts at HSBC Holdings Plc.

Employment is a politically sensitive issue and maintaining social stability is a priority for China’s leadership. Meanwhile, pressures in the labor market are becoming more widespread, even as the overall urban unemployment rate slipped slightly to 5% in June, matching the lowest in a year.

The reading for the employment component of China’s official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index worsened last month, extending a streak of contraction that began in March 2023. An index of future hiring plans fell in June to a nine-month low, according to results of a poll of mostly private companies surveyed by the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business.

See also: China unleashes broad state support to halt tech stock sell-off

Outlays from the unemployment insurance fund, which helps retrain those laid off and pays part of their salaries, jumped to 88.1 billion yuan (US$13 billion or $16.8 billion) in January-May, on par with its expenditures during the pandemic in 2020.

“China’s economy entered the third quarter on a weak footing after sluggish second-quarter growth, reinforcing the case for stronger policy support to meet the annual growth target. High-frequency indicators through July 10 point to soft domestic demand, which could be weighing on production,” said Bloomberg Economics.

As the economic pain builds, the authorities have come under pressure to ramp up stimulus. But for now, many analysts expect them to deliver additional aid only if the situation deteriorates further, opting instead to accelerate the implementation of measures already in the pipeline.

At a Monday meeting of China’s cabinet, top officials said “the efficient use of fiscal funds should be maximised” and vowed to ensure the economy reaches their annual growth target of 4.5%-5%.

A huddle of the ruling Communist Party’s powerful Politburo could provide more clues on what further measures are in the cards later this month. The gathering usually focuses on economic policy in the second half of the year.

“We expect the July Politburo meeting to deliver stronger easing rhetoric,” Hui Shan, chief China economist with Goldman Sachs Group Inc, wrote in a Monday note. The government will prioritise faster disbursement of existing fiscal ammunition such as government bonds, “with further resources possible if needed,” she added.

title: Wall Street talks up carry trade as returns soar most in decades
article:
(July 21): One of the most enduring foreign-exchange bets is off to its best run in decades as surprisingly muted volatility across asset classes has investors piling into carry trades.

The strategy, which involves borrowing in low-yielding currencies to invest where returns are higher, has proven a winner in 2026 as the global economy remains unexpectedly resilient in the face of the oil shock spurred by the Iran war. That backdrop is suppressing market swings and buoying risk appetite among traders seeking out lofty yields in developing nations.

One version that strategists at Citigroup Inc and other banks have been citing lately involves borrowing in euros to buy a basket comprising the Brazilian real, Colombian peso and Turkish lira. It’s up roughly 18% this year through last week, the most year-to-date since 2005, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

Carry has been the strongest strategy for currency traders this year, handily outpacing widely followed alternatives such as the momentum or value approaches. Citigroup, Goldman Sachs Group Inc and JPMorgan Chase & Co are touting it in research, and investors such as Nuveen and Vontobel say it likely has room to run.

“Carry is a gift that has kept giving” even as Mideast tensions flared anew in the past month, JPMorgan strategists led by Meera Chandan said in a research note on Friday. “With foreign-exchange volatility at new cycle lows, our expectation is for carry to continue to deliver.”

See also: Carry trades face best conditions since 2000, Goldman says

Traders traditionally use a variety of currencies to fund the carry strategy, including the dollar and especially the yen, given that interest rates in Japan were around zero for decades. Turning to the euro as the base currency makes sense as a way to diversify, and the region’s benchmark rate, at 2.25%, is lower than the Federal Reserve’s range for its target, of 3.5%-3.75%.

The steadiness this year of the greenback — the world’s major reserve currency — has been a decisive part of the setup for carry, filtering through exchange-rates globally.

See also: India banks slash short-term debt sales on cheaper forex funding

With US inflation cooling more than expected in June and traders increasingly seeing the Fed on hold until later this year, a measure of one-month implied volatility on the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index last week sank to its lowest since December.

“The strategy has worked so far in spite of geopolitical tensions and angst about the glide path of US monetary policy,” said Hari Hariharan, chief executive officer at New York-based hedge fund NWI, who likes a few select carry trades.

He expects high-yielding currencies including Brazil’s real to fare well against the euro, the yen and euro proxies such as the Polish zloty. Brazil’s and Colombia’s currencies have delivered total returns of at least 15% against the dollar this year.

There is, of course, plenty of risk in leaning into the carry trade. Because it relies on picking up incremental bits of yield over time, big moves in exchange rates — like at the outset of the Iran war almost five months ago, or during the tariff shock of early 2025 — can wipe out returns.

Investors don’t have to look back too far for a reminder of how quickly the strategy can unravel.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

In August 2024, a hawkish repricing of Bank of Japan policy triggered a surge in market volatility and drove the yen sharply stronger. That sparked a chaotic scramble to exit leveraged positions as traders rushed to repay loans in the Japanese currency, fueling a brief meltdown in global financial markets.

The yen, which is around its weakest level in decades, is still a major funding currency. Hedge funds’ net short against the yen is close to the biggest since 2007, Commodity Futures Trading Commission data show. However, market watchers say BOJ policy expectations are better priced in than a couple years ago.

“The comparison with the summer of 2024 is instructive but should not be overstated,” said Laura Cooper, global investment strategist and head of macro credit at Nuveen. “A sharper yen rally could still unsettle risk assets broadly, but another disorderly global carry-trade unwind appears less likely.”

At Standard Bank, Steven Barrow says he expects strong carry-trade returns will likely continue for now. However, he’s watching the Fed, where chairman Kevin Warsh has promised an overhaul of communications. Investors anticipate that could mean less forward guidance on policy.

“What we fear most is not just a hike from the Fed, but one that is delivered without any forewarning from Fed members,” the bank’s head of G10 strategy said in a note last week.

Investors worried about the dollar outlook or the threat that Japanese authorities will intervene to support the yen are varying the currencies in which they borrow, turning to the Swiss franc and the Australian dollar, in addition to the euro.

“This ‘all-weather’ approach has historically enabled investors to maintain exposure to the structural EM carry opportunity while avoiding an outright directional stance in what could be an uncertain US dollar environment,” said Thierry Larose, a portfolio manager at Vontobel.

title: Northrop Grumman raises outlook amid record US$105 bil backlog
article:
(July 21): Northrop Grumman Corp raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook amid a flood of new orders that pushed the company’s backlog to record levels.

The defence contractor booked US$20 billion in new contracts during the second quarter, it said in an earnings release on Tuesday, helping expand its backlog to US$105 billion as sales accelerated across all business segments.

Second-quarter sales rose 10% from the previous quarter and 5% from a year earlier, the company said, as the wars in Iran and Ukraine fuelled demand.

The company now expects 2026 sales between US$43.75 billion and US$44.25 billion, an increase of US$250 million over previous estimates, and earnings per share between US$28.60 and US$29.10.

“Northrop Grumman achieved a new record backlog, driven by robust global demand for our products,” CEO Kathy Warden said in the earnings release.

The company made US$7.68 a share in the second quarter, higher than the adjusted and diluted earnings per share of US$6.83 analysts polled by Bloomberg expected on average.

See also: Hasbro beats on sales and raises outlook, buoyed by Magic: The Gathering growth

Major awards in the second quarter included a US$7.6 billion deal for the Sentinel programme, the Air Force’s replacement for the Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile.

The company also netted a US$1 billion contract for work related to the Lockheed Martin Corp F-35 fighter jet within its aeronautics and mission systems divisions and US$800 million for the development of the Glide Phase Interceptor, meant to defeat hypersonic missile threats. Northrop won another US$4.3 billion for restricted programmes.

Sales increased in the second quarter by US$525 million from a year earlier, driven by growth across all business segments including a 13% increase in its aeronautics division.

See also: US stocks, bonds fall as US-Iran risks whipsaw oil

The increase in the aeronautics sector is primarily due to higher production volume on its new bomber, the B-21 Raider.

Operating income totalled US$1.1 billion for the quarter with an operating margin of 10.1%.

title: Data centres on track to suck up a fifth of US power use by 2035
article:
(July 21): Data centres in the US will account for about 20% of the nation’s electricity consumption in 2035, up from 5.9% today, according to BloombergNEF.

That compares with an estimated 12% in 2030, it said in a report Tuesday. In states such as Virginia and Texas, where data centres are concentrated, their share of electricity use will be even higher.

Given the speed at which soaring demand from artificial intelligence is increasing, BNEF projects data centre power needs to reach 194GW in the country by 2035. That’s a jump of 83% from its December forecast. The gain reflects a growing pipeline of AI facilities poised to be built within the next decade. One gigawatt is equivalent to the capacity of a traditional nuclear reactor.

Surging demand from AI data centres is already straining electric grids that are racing to provide enough energy to meet customer needs after two decades of stagnant load growth. That’s forcing companies led by data centre operators to find new ways to power their huge campuses. At the same time, developers face obstacles such as permitting freezes imposed by local governments and political opposition over the projects’ growing energy needs and environmental impacts.

See also: US gasoline prices surpass US$4 a gallon for first time in a month

See also: US consumer sentiment climbs on cheaper gas, tops forecasts

“Every coal plant, every gas plant, every solar farm in the US — one unit of energy out of five generated by them is going to data centres," said Lloyd Arnold, an analyst at BNEF and one of the authors of the report. “So that’s the same energy that’s going to be going into powering electric vehicles, powering cities, et cetera.”

Data centres in areas served by PJM Interconnection LLC, the grid operator covering 13 states including Data Center Alley in Northern Virginia and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas Inc are expected to account for an above-average share of annual electricity use in 2035.

“We’re already seeing the grid struggling to keep up and that’s driving a change in how assets connect to the grid,” Arnold said.

Annually, the record for the amount of data centre capacity that can get connected to the grid is 7.1GW in a single year, according to BNEF. Even if that pace is maintained, the analysts project a 19GW shortfall by 2035 under the base-case scenario, despite additions of on-site gas generation, assuming that demand is served from the on-site gas pipeline.

title: Houthis warn all ships against calling at Saudi Arabia’s ports
article:
(July 21): A message from Yemen’s Houthi rebels to shipowners warned all vessels against calling at Saudi Arabian ports, shedding light on the scope of a threat that puts millions of barrels of exports from the kingdom at risk.

In an email to shipowners, the Iran-backed group makes clear that its blockade doesn’t just apply to Saudi vessels, but to all ships coming to and from Saudi ports, according to the message seen by Bloomberg. It has been months since the Houthis attacked vessels, but they reprised the threat to do so on Monday as the conflict in the Middle East escalated.

“We strongly recommend that your company exercise due diligence and the utmost care in all its dealings, and ensure that no vessel voyages are conducted to or from Saudi ports,” the Houthis said in the email. “Any such activity would expose the violating vessels to sanctions. Furthermore, they may be subject to targeting in any location within the operational reach of the Yemeni Armed Forces.”

The move threatens Saudi oil exports from Yanbu, a Red Sea hub that’s become a crucial workaround since the Iran war brought shipping through the Strait of Hormuz to a near-halt. It’s unclear, however, how effective the blockade will be.

On Monday, an official with an oil tanker in the Red Sea said there was a radio broadcast from “Yemeni armed forces” to shipping in the area, saying that Saudi vessels were blocked. The person said the crew that heard the transmission believed it to be authentic.

See also: Chinese warship conducts rare machine gun test fire in Japan's exclusive economic zone

A Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Monday it has begun implementing operational measures to protect ships in Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry didn’t respond to a request for comments on the emailed message.

The Iran-backed group said on Monday it would place the embargo on Saudi ports as a result of what it says is Saudi Arabia’s siege on the Yemeni capital, Sana’a.

The kingdom has been able to divert large volumes of crude that were previously exported from the Persian Gulf to Yanbu, thanks to an east-west pipeline linking the two coasts. Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a crucial chokepoint connecting the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea.

title: Singapore leads record foreign investments in Southeast Asia
article:
(July 21): Southeast Asia is a “strategic winner” from supply chain shifts and capital reallocation, highlighting the region’s resilience, according to United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB).

Foreign direct investments to the region jumped 10% to a record US$244 billion ($315 billion) in 2025, according to a UOB analysis of the latest data from UN Trade and Development. The increase outpaced the 6% global growth and places Southeast Asia’s total investment capture near Europe’s.

Singapore was the second-most attractive FDI destination after the US, attracting US$151 billion in inflows. Malaysia had the strongest expansion at 51%, supported primarily by investments in digital infrastructure. Thailand and Vietnam also posted gains while FDI in Indonesia fell 14%.

“At first glance, Indonesia’s decline in FDI inflows may raise concerns,” UOB economists Enrico Tanuwidjaja and Vincentius Ming Shen wrote in the report this week. Instead, it appears to mask continued long-term commitments by global investors, they added.

Indonesia has led the region in corporate acquisitions and industrial developments as well as drawing the largest share of large-scale infrastructure financing, according to the economists.

“Although headline FDI inflows showed divergent trends across Asean economies, the region continues to benefit from strong structural investment drivers,” the bank said. These drivers include accelerating focus on digital infrastructure and green industries.

See also: STI at 5,000 and beyond

Asean’s investment gains come as manufacturers continue to diversify some lower-value consumer goods and electronic assembly beyond China, Oxford Economics economists Alexandra Hermann and Artie Lam said in a June 29 report.

title: Hasbro beats on sales and raises outlook, buoyed by Magic: The Gathering growth
article:
(July 21): Hasbro Inc reported second-quarter revenue that beat analysts’ expectations and raised its full-year outlook based on the strength of its Magic: The Gathering card game business, which grew 32% year over year.

“Magic: The Gathering eclipsed US$500 million in quarterly revenue for the first time in its 30-plus-year history,” CEO Chris Cocks said in a press release Tuesday, citing Marvel Super Heroes-themed cards. “The Magic flywheel is firing on all cylinders.”

Hasbro reported a 16% increase in revenue to US$1.14 billion, topping analysts’ expectations of US$1.07 billion. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation came in at US$330.4 million, beating Wall Street estimates of US$297.3 million.

Magic: The Gathering brought in US$545.3 million for the quarter — US$133.3 million more than in the same quarter in 2025. Now, Hasbro expects a 5% to 7% increase in revenue for the full year, up from 3% to 5%.

The company also raised its outlook for adjusted Ebitda to US$1.45 billion to US$1.5 billion, up from US$1.4 billion to US$1.45 billion.

A change to the company’s post-2028 video-game portfolio caused a US$56 million impairment. In May, Bloomberg News reported that Hasbro had cancelled a publishing deal with video-game studio Giant Skull for an action-adventure game set in the Dungeons & Dragons world.

See also: US stocks, bonds fall as US-Iran risks whipsaw oil

title: Chinese warship conducts rare machine gun test fire in Japan's exclusive economic zone
article:
(July 21): A Chinese destroyer conducted a machine gun test around 180km southwest of a Japanese island in the Pacific Ocean, Tokyo’s Defense Ministry said, a rare live-fire exercise by the Chinese navy while inside the exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of Japanese territory.

Two Chinese destroyers were observed sailing with a Russian frigate and a Chinese supply ship approximately 330km southwest of the island of Okinotorishima at around 2am Japanese time on Sunday, according to a statement from the Defense Ministry.

One of the Chinese destroyers was later seen to fire from a machine gun around 180km southwest of the Japanese island, according to the statement.

The ministry said it was the first time that it had announced a live-fire exercise by a foreign navy in Japan’s EEZ.

“The government lodged a protest with China through diplomatic channels, on the grounds that such activity could pose a danger to the navigation of vessels in the surrounding waters,” Japan’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said at a regular press conference on Tuesday.

A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman rejected Japan’s concern, denying that Tokyo has a right to claim an EEZ around Okinotorishima because it is a small maritime feature that is mostly submerged at high tide.

See also: Burnham faces warning Iran War could overshadow ascent to UK PM — Bloomberg

“Japan’s claim of an EEZ around Okinotorishima violates international law,” Lin Jian said at a regular press conference. “China’s activities in the high seas are fully consistent with international law and international practice,” he said.

Ahead of the exercise, the crew of the Chinese destroyer notified nearby vessels about the exercise and its duration ahead of time, Kihara said.

The Chinese navy has become more active around Japan in recent years, often operating alongside Russian military vessels.

See also: Old Middle East, new China

“We view this latest joint transit as part of the broader trend toward closer military coordination between the two countries,” Kihara said.

The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea doesn’t ban naval exercises inside the EEZ of foreign nations, but some countries view such activity as more problematic than others. An EEZ, which extends 200 nautical miles (370km) in the waters around a nation’s land, grants a nation exclusive rights to explore and exploit natural resources in the area.

title: Temasek, BlackRock, Hillhouse said set to back Innolight listing in Hong Kong
article:
(July 21): BlackRock Inc, Hillhouse Investment and Temasek Holdings Pte Ltd are set to be among cornerstone investors in the potential US$8 billion ($10.3 billion) listing by Zhongji Innolight Co in Hong Kong, according to people familiar with the matter.

Investment firms Aspex Management, JPMorgan Asset Management, Wellington Management Co and Jack Ma-backed Yunfeng Capital Co are also planning to participate as cornerstone investors, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

The cornerstone investors are expected to take up almost half of the deal, the people said. Such buyers get guaranteed allocation in exchange for holding the shares for a fixed period, typically six months.

Innolight, the world’s largest maker of optical transceivers that are essential in data centres, is planning to start taking investor orders as soon as Wednesday for what could be Hong Kong’s biggest share sale in seven years, the people said. While the base deal size will be around US$7 billion, the over-allotment option could push it to US$8 billion, they said.

Deliberations are ongoing and details of the offering including the cornerstone line-up may change, the people added.

Hillhouse, JPMorgan Asset Management, Temasek and Aspex declined to comment. BlackRock, Wellington and Yunfeng didn’t respond to emailed queries. Innolight also didn’t respond.

See also: EGP Energy offers 18.82 million shares at 51 cents for IPO

On Monday, Innolight started gauging investor demand for its Hong Kong listing, terms of the deal showed.

At US$8 billion, it would be Hong Kong’s biggest share sale since Alibaba Group Holding Ltd’s US$12.9 billion listing in 2019. Innolight’s offering may also catapult Hong Kong’s listing proceeds this year past the nearly US$37 billion raised in 2025, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The debut is part of a wave of offerings by Chinese companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain that have fuelled this year’s deals boom in Hong Kong. Other sizeable deals in the pipeline include Innolight’s peer Eoptolink Technology Inc, which is preparing to raise as much as US$5 billion, people familiar with the matter have said.

See also: AI pioneer Kai-Fu Lee’s startup targets Hong Kong IPO next year

Innolight’s shares in Shenzhen have surged over 500% in the last year on enthusiasm for companies involved in the buildout of AI. That’s lifted its market value to about US$187 billion and increased the deal size significantly.

However, a sell-off in chipmakers has gathered pace on worries that the AI spending spree is becoming harder to justify. Innolight’s shares have dropped about 18% since a June peak.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc, China International Capital Corp, Morgan Stanley and GF Securities Co are leading Innolight’s listing. Haitong International Securities Co, Citigroup Inc, HSBC Holdings plc and China Galaxy Securities Co are also working on it, according to a filing.

title: Hong Kong court rejects water heiress appeal over US$1.8 bil
article:
(July 21): A Hong Kong court has dismissed a further appeal by the heiress to Hangzhou Wahaha Group Co, preserving two prior orders involving US$1.8 billion ($2.3 billion) in assets held in an HSBC Holdings plc account.

The Court of Appeal rejected Kelly Zong’s bid to challenge earlier rulings and refused her request for more time to file an appeal, according to a judgement handed down on Tuesday. Zong, the daughter of late billionaire Zong Qinghou, was also ordered, along with the other defendant, to pay the plaintiffs’ legal costs of HK$250,000 (US$31,880 or $41,119). The ruling further denied the defendants’ request to suspend parts of an earlier disclosure order, according to the filing.

The 44-year-old applied to the city’s Court of Appeal late last year for permission to challenge a preservation order and a disclosure order previously granted by a High Court judge in August. She is asking the court to set aside both orders and dismiss the originating summons amid an inheritance dispute with three of her half-siblings. The three plaintiffs — Jacky, Jessie and Jerry Zong — are seeking more than US$2 billion in trust assets that they said their late father promised them before he died in February 2024.

Despite the latest setback, Kelly could still make a final attempt at the Court of Final Appeal.

The case has raised eyebrows and lit up on Chinese social media, raising concerns over the country’s succession wave among private enterprises. Kelly, inherited a 29% stake of the the beverage empire founded by her father. She stepped down as Wahaha’s chairwoman and general manager late last year, and now runs a separate beverage producer and packaging business Hongsheng Group, according to Chinese commerce database Qcc.com.

title: MoneyMax Financial Services expects 'significant' improvement in its 1HFY2026 numbers
article:
MoneyMax Financial Services expects to report a "significant" improvement in its 1HFY2026 earnings over the year earlier period.

For the half year ended June 2025, the company reported earnings of $29.6 million, on revenue of $242.3 million, themselves y-o-y improvements of 78.8 and 31.2% respectively.

The company attributes the better showing to the stronger financial performance of its pawnbroking segment, driven by higher interest income from the sustained growth in pledged loan receivables.

Its business of selling and trading gold and luxury items helped as well.

It expects to report on or about Aug 11.

MoneyMax Financial Services gained 4.03% to close at 78 cents on July 21, extending its year to date gain of 64.89%.

title: Burnham appoints first AI minister to cabinet in tech reshuffle
article:
(July 21): Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Kanishka Narayan as minister for artificial intelligence, making the post a cabinet-level position for the first time.

Burnham separately dissolved the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, or DSIT, and merged some of its functions with the Department for Business and Trade. He appointed Jonathan Reynolds as secretary of state, overseeing the newly created Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade.

Narayan’s brief spans the Cabinet Office and Reynolds’s department, according to a government statement. It’s not yet clear how the newly formed departments will handle policies in critical tech areas like data centres, technology procurement, copyright and semiconductors. A DSIT representative declined to comment; the Cabinet Office didn’t return a request for comment.

The Department of Culture, Media and Sport will also expand under Lisa Nandy, overseeing some of the government digital work and tech regulation managed by DSIT.

The response to the restructure was mixed among UK entrepreneurs and investors, who worried about the dissolution of a department focused on their industry but heaped praise on Narayan, the junior minister for AI and online safety since late last year.

In that role, Narayan served under technology secretary Liz Kendall, who was ousted on Monday alongside several senior ministers who served under Starmer. He has announced millions of pounds in investment to UK semiconductor and AI startups and oversees the UK’s AI Security Institute, one of the first international organisations to test Anthropic PBC’s cutting-edge Mythos model.

See also: Burnham vows ‘hope and unity’ as he prepares to take power in UK

Moving oversight of digital services to the culture department “feels like a return to the early 2000s, when technology was treated as a curious side interest rather than a core part of economic growth,” said Alexandru Voica, head of public affairs for Synthesia, a prominent AI startup based in London.

Startup Coalition, a London-based advocacy group, wrote a letter to Burnham over the weekend saying DSIT’s closure would shut the “single front door” the tech sector had to the government. “The abolition of DSIT is clearly a bad thing,” Dom Hallas, the organisation's executive director, said after Burnham’s changes. “But if anyone could make up for it in cabinet, it would be Kanishka [Narayan], who knows startups and the ecosystem better than anyone in government.”

The UK’s position as a quantum computing cluster is also at risk after the restructure and resignation of science minister Patrick Vallance, said Dame Anne Glover, CEO of investment firm Amadeus Capital Partners. “All of that was very visible because of that department and in particular Patrick Vallance,” she said. Vallance resigned from DSIT on Monday, citing personal reasons.

See also: London offices without air-conditioning become ‘extremely’ hard to lease

Narayan’s elevation is a “reassuring counter-signal” to the DSIT closure, said Meryem Arik, co-founder of British AI startup Doubleword. He “is trusted in Whitehall and in industry alike as an operator who can actually get things done", she added.

Britain isn’t the first G7 nation to appoint a high-level AI minister, with France and Canada establishing similar roles over the last two years.

“Nations have a narrow window to decide whether they shape AI or get shaped by it,” Narayan wrote on X after he was named to the cabinet. “Britain is in that window right now.”

The UK’s artificial intelligence strategy is being watched closely beyond its borders. It is home to a swath of venture capitalists, prominent AI operators — including Google DeepMind and startups like ElevenLabs and Wayve — as well as a coveted engineering talent pool. After Brexit, the country tried positioning itself as a welcome hub for overseas tech investment, with a lighter regulatory touch than the European Union.

Still, Britain’s leaders have faced criticism for flip-flopping on tech initiatives and underinvesting in computing resources. Some marquee digital infrastructure projects, including a planned OpenAI data centre, have been cancelled or put on hold, in part because of the country’s high energy prices.

Burnham, who took over on Monday after Starmer resigned this summer, has said little about his AI and tech strategy. A critical area that DSIT had managed was copyright law. The country has abandoned setting new rules that would determine how companies training AI models could use protected material.

Burnham and Narayan will also be forced to take a position on the tech sovereignty debate in Europe. Officials in France and Germany want the continent to rely as little as possible on models and software from Silicon Valley, a call fuelled by Washington’s willingness to cut off foreign access to cutting-edge models.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

DSIT was formed in 2023 by Starmer’s predecessor, Conservative leader Rishi Sunak. The department has backed research programmes in quantum computing and clean energy.

It also set up AI Growth Zones, designated areas for building data centres with approval processes and access to power. One of the first big projects — a campus from OpenAI and British cloud provider Nscale — hit a snag earlier this year after the ChatGPT creator pulled out, citing regulation and high energy costs.

At the time, Narayan pushed back on the idea that Britain’s rules and electricity prices would restrict large data centres.

The department oversaw the creation of the Sovereign AI Fund, a €500 million state-backed venture unit that has invested in a handful of British AI companies, including Ineffable Intelligence — a new AI model developer from a DeepMind alum — and Alphabet Inc’s Isomorphic Labs.
